name: Health System
description: Iran’s health system connects national health policy, medical education, and regional service management through the Ministry of Health and Medical Education and universities of medical sciences. Its community health network is central to primary care, while financing, workforce management, and coordination remain important areas of reform.

seo.title: Iran’s Health System: Institutions, Primary Care and Reform | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s health system, from community health workers and medical universities to national governance, financing reform, and coordination challenges.

content.heading: A health system with universities at its center
content.content:
A useful starting point for understanding Iran’s health system is the relationship between government, universities, and local services. The Ministry of Health and Medical Education handles national policy and planning; state universities of medical sciences oversee services within regional networks. These universities therefore have responsibilities that extend beyond classrooms, laboratories, and teaching hospitals. They help organize the delivery of health care to surrounding communities. Research describes this administrative structure at national, provincial, and county levels. [s1]

This arrangement connects two different activities: preparing health professionals and managing the services in which they work. It also makes the medical university an important institution for understanding local health administration. A university’s educational reputation and its responsibilities for population health are related aspects of its role, rather than interchangeable measures of success. [s1]

content.heading: Community care and the rural–urban distinction
content.content:
Primary health care means accessible first-contact care combined with prevention and continuing support for population health. In Iran, its best-known community worker is the **behvarz**, whose work forms part of the rural health-house network. WHO’s historical case-study overview identifies the development, training, and supervision of these workers as important to the expansion of health services, particularly for rural communities. It associates the network’s development with improvements in maternal and child health and life expectancy. These are historical assessments, rather than a guarantee of identical services in every locality today. [s2]

The network takes different forms across settlements. Rural communities are served through health houses and rural comprehensive health centers; urban services include health posts and urban comprehensive health centers. The distinction matters when interpreting references to a local “health center”: the term does not necessarily describe the same facility, staffing arrangement, or role everywhere. [s1]

content.heading: Access also depends on financing
content.content:
An extensive service network does not by itself settle who pays for treatment or how well households are protected from its cost. WHO’s 2020 financing and governance assessment describes reform efforts addressing insurance coverage, patient cost-sharing, benefit packages, and the purchasing of services. Purchasing here means deciding which services to pay for, from which providers, and under what arrangements. [s3]

The assessment places the Health Transformation Plan within this broader reform history. Its scope shows why health-system performance cannot be judged from hospital construction or insurance enrollment alone: service availability, financial protection, purchasing arrangements, and governance all require attention. The report presents policy options for further progress toward universal health coverage; its discussion should not be read as confirmation that every reform objective was achieved or remains implemented in the same form. [s3]

content.heading: Formal structure and practical performance
content.content:
Evidence from practitioners and researchers complicates a purely organizational account. A qualitative study published in 2022 identified problems involving governance, personnel, resources, financial management, service delivery, and collaboration beyond the health sector. Its interviews provide evidence about perceived implementation difficulties, not national estimates of how frequently each problem occurs. [s1]

The COVID-19 response also demonstrated how community services could support emergency care. WHO described primary-care teams using telephone follow-up, community records, and triage to help identify suspected cases and direct people toward further assessment. These were documented pandemic-response activities, rather than evidence that every digital tool or procedure continued unchanged afterward. [s4]

The central distinction is between having a connected institutional framework and making its connections work consistently. Iran’s system is best understood by examining community services, regional management, and national financing together, while keeping historical achievements separate from present-day measures of access and quality. [s1][s3][s4]

name: Ministry of Health
description: Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education combines national health responsibilities with oversight of medical education. Its institutional history links professional training to service delivery, with universities of medical sciences playing an important intermediary role.

seo.title: Iran’s Ministry of Health and Medical Education | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore why Iran’s health ministry also oversees medical education, how that arrangement developed, and what it means for governance and accountability.

content.heading: Why medical education is in the ministry’s name
content.content:
The institution commonly shortened in English to Iran’s Ministry of Health is more fully the **Ministry of Health and Medical Education**, often abbreviated MoHME. The longer title captures a consequential administrative choice: medical training and health services were brought into the same ministerial framework. A WHO regional document dates the parliamentary approval of this integration to 1985. It describes the transfer of health-related educational institutions from the higher-education ministry into the health ministry. [s1]

For international readers, this helps explain why a medical university can appear in accounts of local health administration as well as academic research. The ministry’s educational responsibilities are part of the architecture of service delivery, rather than simply a separate interest in university qualifications. [s1]

content.heading: Integration developed in stages
content.content:
The merger was followed by further organizational changes. WHO’s 2006 account describes provincial health organizations initially operating alongside medical universities. It then identifies their integration in 1994 as another major step, bringing education, research, and regional health-service responsibilities together. These dates explain the formation of the model; they do not establish the present details of every university’s jurisdiction. [s1]

The distinction between organizational integration and effective cooperation remains significant. Research published in 2025 examined expert perspectives on the arrangement and identified incomplete functional integration, management problems, and communication barriers. Its findings suggest that placing activities under one institutional umbrella does not automatically make research, teaching, and service management work together effectively. [s2]

content.heading: Educational oversight and accreditation
content.content:
Medical education also requires mechanisms for assessing training quality. FAIMER’s Directory of Organizations that Recognize or Accredit Medical Schools identifies the Secretariat of the Council for Undergraduate Medical Education as a governmental body within MoHME. Its listed accreditation concerns include curriculum, clinical teaching, and examination regulations. The evaluation process includes institutional self-study, site visits, resource review, and discussions with students and staff. [s3]

The directory distinguishes recognition of the accrediting agency from accreditation of individual schools. Recognition by the World Federation for Medical Education does not mean that every medical school in Iran is accredited by that agency. School-specific claims therefore require school-specific evidence. [s3]

content.heading: Reading the ministry’s role critically
content.content:
The ministry’s broad remit makes coordination an important question for evaluating its work. The 2025 integration study argues for clearer processes, stronger monitoring, and more consistent use of evidence in decision-making. Those are research recommendations, rather than completed administrative reforms. Because the study draws on selected policymakers and key informants, it illuminates institutional debates without independently measuring all health-system outcomes. [s2]

The ministry is consequently best understood through both its formal responsibilities and evidence about implementation. Its combined mandate explains how the system is organized; judging its effectiveness requires additional evidence about education, services, and population health. [s1][s2]

name: Medical Universities
description: Iran’s universities of medical sciences combine professional education and research with important responsibilities for health services. Their integrated role connects academic institutions to hospitals and community health networks, while creating practical tensions between educational and service priorities.

seo.title: Medical Universities in Iran: Education, Research and Health Services | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Learn how Iran’s medical universities connect professional training, research, hospitals, and community services, and why integration remains debated.

content.heading: More than a collection of medical schools
content.content:
In Iran, a university of medical sciences can be both an academic institution and an organization responsible for health services. Understanding that combination prevents a common misreading: references to a university in public-health administration do not necessarily concern students or a campus. They may concern the institution’s wider service responsibilities. WHO’s historical account describes education, research, and regional health care being joined within universities of medical sciences and health services. [s1]

That arrangement developed through successive reforms. Following the national integration of medical education and health administration, provincial health organizations initially remained alongside universities. Their merger in 1994 consolidated responsibilities within the university-based structure. The historical sequence helps explain why institutional names often refer to both medical sciences and health services. [s1]

content.heading: What integration is intended to connect
content.content:
The educational argument for integration is that training and research should respond to the needs encountered in health services. A qualitative study published in 2025 describes expert views of integration in terms of community responsiveness, links between researchers and decision-makers, and closer connections among education, research, and treatment. This is a statement of intended relationships, rather than proof that all institutions achieve them equally. [s2]

The same study identifies a gap between organizational merger and functional integration. Experts reported communication problems and insufficient planning for how the different activities should work together. Their accounts suggest that sharing an institution is only a starting point: cooperation depends on processes that connect academic work with service decisions. [s2]

content.heading: When service demands compete with teaching
content.content:
Integration brings competing priorities into the same organization. A scoping review published in 2024 examined the educational dimensions of Iran’s model. Its accessible English abstract reports benefits involving workforce development and more socially oriented education, alongside concerns that treatment receives greater attention than education and that research funding is inadequate. [s3]

The authors’ conclusion is qualified: they regard integration as having achieved important original objectives, while arguing that education and research have benefited less than service provision. This is the review’s interpretation of the literature, not a uniform assessment of every university or teaching hospital. Only the published abstract was inspected for these findings; detailed claims about individual included studies are therefore not presented here. [s3]

content.heading: An institutional resource during emergencies
content.content: The universities’ service role also matters during public-health emergencies. WHO’s account of Iran’s COVID-19 response describes the medical-university network as a source of specialist expertise within the wider health system. It situates this capacity alongside community-based prevention and primary care. The example illustrates how academic and operational resources can be mobilized together, without establishing that institutional integration alone determined the effectiveness of the response. [s4]

content.heading: Assess institutions and qualifications separately
content.content:
A university’s service responsibilities, research activity, and medical-school accreditation answer different questions. FAIMER identifies a ministry-based accrediting body for undergraduate medical education and lists curriculum, clinical teaching, and examinations among its areas of assessment. Its explicit warning is useful: international recognition of that accrediting agency does not establish that every school in the country is accredited. [s5]

For readers comparing institutions, the practical lesson is to identify the specific school, program, and claim being assessed. The university-based system explains a shared organizational model; it does not replace institution-specific evidence about training quality or accreditation. [s5]
